newsitem.title: USA: U.S. crude outlook-technicals in the driver's seat.
newsitem.headline: U.S. crude outlook-technicals in the driver's seat.

text.p: U.S. crude fundamentals are likely to take a backseat to bullish technicals and the whims of heating oil this week, traders and analysts said Monday.

Fundamentals appear relatively sloppy, due to healthy amounts of domestic oil and no shortfall of imports, but a stalled Iraqi oil-for-food plan and other weather factors are continuing to override demand and supply.
"Crude oil prices now reflect more than the absence of Iraqi oil because there will be a build in the fourth quarter anyway," William Brown, president of W.H. Brown & Co. said.

"I don't see prices dropping to that level. Potential unrest in the Middle East means the market will not be able to relax," Brown added, noting Iraq's foray into northern Kurdish regions and bombings in Saudi Arabia stoked rallies.
The spurt in European gas oil last week, which hauled U.S. heating oil values up and encouraged better refining margins, also lent a similar bullish pattern for crude.

"Product inventories are not all that high but it looks like there are ample crude supplies," said Ken Haley, manager of Chevron Corp's crude oil forecasting unit, adding that in spite of good crude supplies, prices were relatively firm.
High refinery output to meet winter fuel demand and the season's series of hurricanes, could pack more punch to an already technically bullish market.
Overall, traders agreed that West Texas Intermediate was inflated and inconsistent with the supply scenario.

"Refiners continue to pay these prices even without a gun held to their heads," a Texas trader said, noting that both Brent and WTI were not far from five-year highs and both were well above normal levels against sour Persian Gulf crudes.
But domestic crudes retained a competitive edge to imports due to a narrower Atlantic arbitrage and costly freight.
Several million-barrel shipments from the North Sea for October were sighted last week, but traders expect these to be minimized with the arbitrage now only at $1.17 a barrel.
Foreign crudes into the U.S. fell last week to 6.7 million barrels per day (bpd), down from 8.4 million bpd previously.

Traders said there were signs imports headed for the U.S. Gulf had begun to slow, aggravated also by diminished supplies from Colombia and Ecuador, where flows were reduced because of sabotage and ongoing production-sharing negotiations.
